content.text:
## Bottom line

**This is a good, market-rate Google L6 offer—but not yet a compelling offer for someone who is happy at Meta.**

My recommendation:

1. **Do not accept as-is yet.**
2. **Negotiate aggressively but credibly.**
3. **Don’t walk away before giving Google an opportunity to improve it.**
4. If Google makes little or no movement, **staying at Meta is financially reasonable**, particularly if compensation is the main motivation.

## What the offer is actually worth

Using the grant’s four-year average:

| Component | Google |
|---|---:|
| Base | $235,000 |
| Target bonus | $47,000 |
| Annualized RSUs | $270,000 |
| **Normalized annual TC** | **$552,000** |

Compared with your approximately **$526,000 current run-rate**, that is:

- **$26,000 more per year**
- Approximately **5% higher**
- Four-year Google value: **$2.208 million**
- Four years at your current run-rate: **$2.104 million**
- Difference: only **$104,000 over four years**, before stock movement, refreshers, promotions, or bonus variation

That is not a large premium for changing companies when:

- You are happy where you are.
- Google approached you.
- You take on team, manager, performance and reorganization risk.
- Your base salary would decline.
- Google refresh grants are uncertain.
- You are forfeiting approximately $200,000 of Meta equity over the next 12 months.

Your offer is almost exactly the reported Bay Area median for Google L6 PMs: Levels.fyi currently reports roughly **$551,500 median annual compensation**. A recent US dataset reported an L6 median base around $240,000 and median annual stock around $230,000, although these are self-reported data. In other words, your equity is relatively healthy, but the overall package is essentially a median offer rather than a premium passive-candidate offer. ([levels.fyi](https://www.levels.fyi/companies/google/salaries/product-manager/locations/san-francisco-bay-area?utm_source=openai))

## First confirm the vesting schedule

This is crucial. Public sources currently conflict: some report straight 25/25/25/25 vesting, while others report Google’s front-loaded 38/32/20/10 schedule. Alphabet officially says RSUs generally vest over four years, but your written grant terms control. ([levels.fyi](https://www.levels.fyi/companies/google/salaries/product-manager/locations/san-francisco-bay-area?utm_source=openai))

If it is straight-line, your annual compensation before refreshers is approximately:

| Year | TC |
|---|---:|
| 1 | $552,000 |
| 2 | $552,000 |
| 3 | $552,000 |
| 4 | $552,000 |

If it is 38/32/20/10:

| Year | Equity vesting | TC before refreshers |
|---|---:|---:|
| 1 | $410,400 | **$692,400** |
| 2 | $345,600 | **$627,600** |
| 3 | $216,000 | **$498,000** |
| 4 | $108,000 | **$390,000** |

The four-year total is identical, but the retention cliff is completely different. Do not evaluate the offer from the recruiter’s “first-year TC” number until you know this.

Your Meta compensation over the next 12 months, using the more precise $200,000 vesting figure, is approximately **$476,000**. Thus Google’s first-year advantage is either roughly $76,000 under straight-line vesting or substantially more under front-loaded vesting—subject to start date, bonus proration and first vest timing.

## What I would ask for

### Opening counter

Ask for:

- **Base: $260,000**
- **New-hire RSUs: $1.35 million**
- **Sign-on bonus: $200,000**

This is intentionally an anchor, not necessarily the expected outcome.

Why it is defensible:

- $260,000 is below the posting’s stated $271,000 maximum.
- The $200,000 sign-on directly corresponds to documented Meta equity vesting you are walking away from.
- $1.35 million in equity is only 25% above their initial grant.
- You are a passive candidate who already has comparable compensation and is happy at a direct competitor.

That package would have a normalized recurring value around:

- $260,000 base
- $52,000 target bonus
- $337,500 annualized equity
- **$649,500 recurring annual TC**
- Plus the one-time signing bonus

You may not get all of that, but it establishes that Google needs to pay a meaningful switching premium.

### A strong realistic landing point

I would consider this a successful negotiation:

- **Base: $250,000–$255,000**
- **RSUs: $1.2 million–$1.3 million**
- **Sign-on: $100,000–$150,000**

For example:

- $250,000 base
- $50,000 target bonus
- $1.3 million RSUs, or $325,000 annualized
- **$625,000 normalized recurring TC**
- Plus a signing bonus

That is approximately a 19% recurring premium over your stated Meta run-rate—much more appropriate for an unsolicited move.

A lower but still reasonable result would be:

- $250,000 base
- $1.2 million RSUs
- $100,000+ sign-on

That produces approximately **$600,000 normalized annual TC**, plus the sign-on.

## Which components to prioritize

If Google cannot improve everything, prioritize as follows:

### 1. New-hire equity

Increasing the grant from $1.08 million to $1.3 million adds $220,000 of four-year value, or $55,000 annually on a straight-line basis.

This does expose you to Alphabet share-price risk, but it creates the largest recurring compensation improvement.

### 2. Sign-on bonus

You have a concrete, documented reason for a make-whole payment: $200,000 vesting at Meta over the next 12 months.

Ask for the entire $200,000. If they resist, try to land at **$100,000–$150,000**. Ask whether it can be split across two payments if Google has a first-year limit—for example, $100,000 at joining and $50,000 after 12 months.

### 3. Base salary

At minimum, ask Google to **match your $240,000 Meta base**. Preferably land at $250,000 or higher.

Base is especially valuable because it is guaranteed and also increases the dollar value of the 20% target bonus. Nevertheless, salary bands may make equity and sign-on easier levers for the recruiter.

## Suggested wording

You can say this on a call and follow up in writing:

> I’m genuinely excited about the team and the opportunity. At the same time, I wasn’t actively looking and I’m happy at Meta, so the financial case needs to be compelling for me to take on the risk of a move.
>
> My current annual compensation is approximately $526,000, and I would also be walking away from about $200,000 of Meta equity vesting over the next 12 months. On a four-year normalized basis, the current Google offer is approximately $552,000 annually, so it represents only about a 5% recurring increase and does not include a make-whole payment.
>
> Given that, I’d like to request a base salary of $260,000, a new-hire equity grant of $1.35 million, and a $200,000 signing bonus to address the equity I’m forfeiting. I understand there may be constraints among the different components, and I’m open to discussing how to structure the package, but I would need a materially stronger overall package to make the move.

If true, add:

> If we can get the package to the right place, I would be prepared to make a decision promptly.

Do **not** say you will definitely accept unless you mean it.

## How to treat refresh grants

Treat refreshers as **zero in your decision model until granted**.

Google’s own compensation-process description confirms that equity refresh recommendations are part of the annual pay cycle and depend on factors such as performance, location and role, with manager discretion and higher-level review. That means refreshers are real, but neither their amount nor receipt is contractually assured. ([services.google.com](https://services.google.com/fh/files/blogs/pay_equity_info_sheet.pdf?utm_source=openai))

Ask the recruiter:

- When would you first become eligible for a refresh?
- What has been the typical—not guaranteed—refresh range for an L6 PM with a solid rating?
- What vesting schedule do refresh grants use?
- Would joining late in the year reduce or eliminate eligibility for the next cycle?
- Do refreshers begin vesting immediately or after a delay?

Use the answers for context, but don’t count them as guaranteed compensation.

## Before accepting, get these details in writing

1. Exact RSU vesting percentages by year.
2. First vest date and vesting frequency.
3. How the $1.08 million is converted into shares and the applicable grant-date pricing methodology.
4. Whether the first bonus is prorated.
5. First-year bonus payment date.
6. First refresh-review eligibility date.
7. Sign-on repayment terms if they add one.
8. Whether a delayed start date can let additional Meta equity vest.
9. Whether Google will accommodate a start date immediately after a major Meta vest.

Start-date negotiation could itself be worth a significant amount and may be easier to approve than another $50,000 of cash.

## Accept, negotiate or walk?

### **Negotiate now**

The offer is strong enough to engage with, but not strong enough to accept without a counter.

### **Accept if:**

- The role is at least as attractive as your Meta role, **and**
- They get recurring normalized compensation near **$600,000–$625,000**, or
- They provide a substantial $100,000–$200,000 make-whole payment that makes a somewhat lower recurring package worthwhile.

### **Consider accepting as-is only if:**

- The Google role materially improves your career trajectory, domain, manager or promotion prospects, or
- The vesting is heavily front-loaded and you value the near-term liquidity, or
- You independently want to leave Meta.

### **Stay at Meta if:**

- Google barely moves,
- The role itself is not clearly better,
- Compensation is the primary reason you would switch, or
- The team or manager carries meaningful uncertainty.

**My overall judgment:** the current offer is fair but not compelling. Counter at **$260,000 base, $1.35 million equity and $200,000 sign-on**, with a practical objective of landing around **$250,000–$255,000 base, $1.2 million–$1.3 million equity and $100,000–$150,000 sign-on**.

content.text:
## My recommendation: **lean accept**

Financially, Google has now turned this from a merely fair offer into a **compelling four-year package**. Assuming you’re reasonably positive about the role, manager, and team, **I would take it**.

I would stay at Meta only if you substantially prefer your current job or believe your Meta compensation/promotion trajectory will meaningfully outperform the numbers you provided.

## The updated economics

### Recurring compensation

| Component | Meta | Google |
|---|---:|---:|
| Base | $240,000 | $240,000 |
| Target/typical bonus | $36,000 | $48,000 |
| Annualized initial equity | $250,000 | $270,000 |
| **Recurring annual TC** | **$526,000** | **$558,000** |

Google’s recurring advantage is still modest:

- **+$32,000 per year**
- Approximately **6% higher**

But the $200,000 sign-on changes the overall switching economics.

### Four-year comparison

Assuming your Meta compensation remains at the stated $526,000 run rate:

|  | Four-year value |
|---|---:|
| Stay at Meta | **$2,104,000** |
| Join Google, including sign-on | **$2,432,000** |
| **Google advantage** | **$328,000** |

That is about a **15.6% four-year premium**, or approximately **$82,000 more per year averaged across four years**.

That is a legitimate switching premium—not an enormous one, but sufficient for a lateral move between strong companies.

## Your first 12 months are especially strong

You said the next 12 months at Meta would produce approximately:

- $240,000 base
- $36,000 bonus
- $200,000 vesting equity
- **$476,000 total**

If Google’s grant vests 25% in the first year, Google produces approximately:

- $240,000 base
- $48,000 target bonus
- $270,000 equity
- $200,000 sign-on
- **$758,000 total**

That is a **$282,000 first-year advantage** before differences in stock performance and bonus results.

If the grant is front-loaded, the first-year figure could be higher, but only the written vesting schedule should be used. Alphabet states that its RSUs generally vest over four years and require continued employment through the vesting dates. ([abc.xyz](https://abc.xyz/assets/99/21/46cafdba41089a12a2d86ea47d44/goog026-annualreport2024-web.pdf?utm_source=openai))

## Why I’d accept

Google has addressed the three main weaknesses of the original offer:

1. **Your base is no longer decreasing.**
2. **The forfeited Meta equity has been fully matched on a pretax dollar-for-dollar basis.**
3. **You retain a modest recurring compensation increase after the sign-on year.**

You also successfully converted a nonguaranteed future possibility—refresh grants—into **$200,000 of contractual upfront compensation**. That is an excellent negotiation result.

You could reasonably conclude that $32,000 of additional recurring annual compensation alone would not justify moving. But you aren’t receiving only $32,000 more—you are also receiving the $200,000 switching premium. Over the grant’s four-year horizon, the package is meaningful.

## The main reason to decline

The argument for staying is not that the Google offer is financially weak. It is that **you are already happy at Meta**, while switching introduces:

- Manager and team risk
- Performance-rating risk
- Reorganization or layoff risk
- Loss of internal reputation and relationships
- A new promotion clock
- Uncertainty around refresh grants
- Potentially longer commute or less favorable working arrangements

If the Google role feels like a downgrade in scope, product quality, manager, promotion prospects, or lifestyle, the $328,000 projected four-year premium may not compensate for that.

I would therefore use this decision rule:

- **Role/team roughly equal or better:** Accept Google.
- **Google role moderately worse or considerably riskier:** Stay at Meta.
- **You strongly prefer Meta and would be moving almost exclusively for money:** The offer is good enough, but not so overwhelming that declining would be irrational.

## One important caveat: Google’s compensation cliff

The $558,000 figure is the **four-year average of the initial grant**, not necessarily your compensation in each year.

If the grant uses 38%/32%/20%/10% vesting, for example, compensation before refreshers would look roughly like this:

| Year | Base + target bonus | Initial grant vest | Sign-on | Total |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | $288,000 | $410,400 | $200,000 | **$898,400** |
| 2 | $288,000 | $345,600 | — | **$633,600** |
| 3 | $288,000 | $216,000 | — | **$504,000** |
| 4 | $288,000 | $108,000 | — | **$396,000** |

That makes refresh grants important for Years 3–5. Because the recruiter explicitly said refreshes are not guaranteed, continue valuing them at zero when making the decision. In practice, they are potential upside—not part of the offer.

If the grant vests 25% each year, compensation is much smoother: approximately $558,000 annually before the sign-on.

## Before signing

Confirm these items in the actual documents:

1. **Exact vesting schedule and first vest date**
2. **When the $200,000 is paid**
3. **Whether your first bonus is prorated**
4. **Sign-on repayment period**
5. **Whether repayment is prorated monthly**
6. **What happens if Google terminates you without cause or eliminates your role**
7. **Whether repayment means the gross or net amount**
8. **Your first refresh-review eligibility date**
9. **Whether you can time your start after any imminent Meta vest**

For the sign-on, I would especially want language under which:

- The obligation declines proportionally over time.
- No repayment is due if Google terminates you without cause.
- The repayment period is no longer than one year, ideally.
- You are not forced to repay $200,000 gross after receiving substantially less than that net of withholding.

California sharply limits employers’ ability to make deductions from final wages, but that does not necessarily eliminate a separate contractual repayment claim, so the written terms still matter. ([dir.ca.gov](https://dir.ca.gov/dlse/faq_deductions.htm?utm_source=openai))

## Should you negotiate again?

**No—not for more compensation.**

They granted the entire $200,000 make-whole you requested and called it final. Continuing to push risks creating unnecessary friction for relatively little expected return.

It is still appropriate to negotiate or clarify:

- Start date
- Sign-on clawback language
- Work location expectations
- Team assignment
- Any planned vacation
- Timing relative to a near-term Meta vest

Those are acceptance details, not reopening the compensation negotiation.

## Final verdict

**Take it if the role and manager clear a basic “I would be comfortable working here” threshold.**

You achieved:

- Equal base
- Higher target bonus
- Slightly higher annualized initial equity
- Full replacement of the Meta equity you identified as being forfeited
- Approximately **$328,000 more projected pretax compensation over four years**

That is a strong outcome. I would not walk away over compensation at this point; I would decline only because I materially preferred the actual job at Meta.
